addressed_problems.content: While sparsification methods such as Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) and Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) have been shown to correlate with improved plasticity indicators (lower neuron dormancy, higher effective rank, and stabilized Fisher trace) and enhanced multi-task performance in architectures like MTPPO and MoE, the causal mechanisms by which these sparsification-induced plasticity changes lead to performance gains have not been established. The present study reports consistent correlations but does not prove that the measured plasticity metrics directly mediate the performance improvements, leaving open the question of whether these indicators are merely correlated epiphenomena or true mediators of the observed performance enhancements in multi-task reinforcement learning.

The observed benefits of dynamic sparsification (GMP and SET) in multi-task reinforcement learning have been interpreted through concepts such as convergence to flatter minima, L0 regularization, and reduced model degrees of freedom, but formal theoretical explanations of why and under which conditions these sparsification methods lead to flatter minima, sustained plasticity, and improved adaptation in MTRL have not been derived. This represents an open theoretical problem that the authors explicitly identify as future work, requiring a deeper understanding of the optimization landscape and the interplay between sparsity, curvature, and plasticity in multi-task settings.

Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) relies on a random regrowth heuristic to introduce new connections after pruning, which may not consistently yield optimal connectivity patterns for multi-task learning. The open question is whether guided or topology-aware regrowth strategies—potentially informed by task structure, gradient signals, or task-specific importance measures—could further enhance adaptation, reduce negative interference, and improve performance across MTRL architectures, especially given that the random nature of SET's regrowth may limit its effectiveness in complex multi-task environments.

Practical deployment of dynamic sparsification methods in MTRL faces significant challenges: Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) does not reduce training-time computational or memory costs because it operates on dense weight matrices with masks, with true benefits only realized at inference on specialized hardware; Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) can maintain true sparsity during training but its implementation for convolutional or recurrent layers remains complex and not widely available. These limitations motivate research into efficient sparse-training implementations and hardware-software co-design tailored for multi-task reinforcement learning to make sparsification practically viable beyond fully connected layers.

Dynamic sparsification methods (GMP and SET) introduce additional hyperparameters—such as pruning window, sparsity target, pruning frequency, evolution frequency, and regrowth fraction—whose optimal values are architecture- and benchmark-dependent, as demonstrated by the varying performance of GMP and SET across MTPPO, MoE, and MOORE architectures. Characterizing this hyperparameter sensitivity systematically and developing principled guidelines, adaptive tuning mechanisms, or robust default configurations remains an open engineering and scientific problem for the practical application of sparsification in MTRL.

The empirical findings on sparsification-driven plasticity improvements in MTRL are limited to the evaluated benchmarks (MiniGrid MT3/5/7 and MetaWorld MT10) and architectures (MTPPO, MoE, MOORE, MTMH-SAC). Open questions remain about generalization to other observational modalities (e.g., pixel-based inputs, recurrent architectures), larger task suites, longer training horizons, and the precise thresholds at which aggressive pruning (e.g., 99% sparsity) causes irrecoverable representational collapse, as observed in the MOORE architecture where rank collapse and performance degradation occurred at extreme sparsity levels.

Multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) requires a single agent to learn policies that perform well across a distribution of distinct tasks, often with conflicting objectives; this setting amplifies the need for sustained representational flexibility (plasticity) because the network must continually accommodate diverse task-specific mappings and avoid negative task interference. Prior empirical and theoretical work on plasticity loss—characterized by phenomena such as neuron dormancy (many neurons becoming effectively inactive), representational collapse (low-dimensional or highly correlated feature representations), and brittleness to parameter perturbations (high sensitivity as measured by curvature proxies)—has focused mostly on single-task reinforcement learning or continual learning, leaving a gap in understanding how these pathologies manifest and can be mitigated in the multi-task regime. Existing interventions fall into disparate categories—explicit parameter manipulations (e.g., reinitialization of dormant neurons or periodic layer resets), implicit regularization (weight decay, normalization layers), and sparsification/pruning techniques—but their relative effectiveness, mechanisms of action, and interactions with multi-task architectures (shared backbones, Mixture-of-Experts, orthogonal-expert designs) have not been systematically compared under consistent MTRL benchmarks. As a consequence, practitioners lack: (1) a clear empirical assessment of whether modern sparsification strategies that proved useful in single-task RL (e.g., Gradual Magnitude Pruning, Sparse Evolutionary Training) can preserve or restore plasticity in MTRL; (2) quantitative evidence about how changes in plasticity indicators (dormant neuron percentage, effective rank of representations, Fisher Information trace) map onto multi-task performance; and (3) guidance on how architecture choice and sparsity schedules interact—e.g., whether sparsification is uniformly beneficial across architectures or whether it can induce failure modes such as rank collapse under aggressive pruning. This uncertainty prevents principled adoption of sparsity-driven interventions in MTRL, limits reproducible benchmarking across environments of varying observability and action spaces, and leaves open whether observed plasticity improvements are mere correlations or reflect causal mechanisms that can be leveraged to build more adaptable multi-task agents.

nodes.content: In MTRL, sustaining the capacity to adapt (plasticity) is crucial because networks must represent and discriminate features useful across multiple tasks; yet dense overparameterized networks frequently exhibit plasticity‑loss symptoms during training (high neuron dormancy, low effective rank, and volatile sensitivity measures), which impede continued learning and exacerbate negative task interference. Prior mitigation strategies focused either on single-task pruning results, explicit parameter interventions that target individual symptoms (e.g., reinitializing dormant neurons), or on implicit regularizers (weight decay, normalization), but no systematic empirical account existed that (a) applies dynamic sparsification schedules to MTRL architectures, (b) quantifies their effect on multiple, complementary plasticity indicators, and (c) compares their characteristic dynamics across actor and critic parts and across architectures. Without this, it remained unclear whether sparsification would simply compress representations or whether it could actively preserve the network's ability to learn new task-related information in the multi-task context.

Practitioners commonly assume that increasing parameter count or relying on a dense multi-task model is the default route to capacity for solving multiple tasks, but overparameterization can leave large parts of networks underutilized and susceptible to optimization pathologies that limit generalization and adaptation. Although prior single-task RL work showed that pruning can match or exceed dense performance, the multi-task setting introduces additional failure modes (conflicting gradients, negative transfer) and different resource-sharing trade-offs; therefore, empirical evidence was lacking on whether sparsity can both preserve plasticity and translate into higher aggregated multi-task returns across representative MTRL architectures and standardized benchmarks. This gap limited confidence in adopting sparsification as a general strategy for improving multi-task performance rather than merely compressing models.

Multi-task architectures differ in how they allocate capacity and separate task-specific processing (e.g., shared backbone with task heads versus modular expert-based splittings with orthogonality constraints). Prior to this work, there was no systematic characterization of how dynamic sparsification methods interact with these differing inductive biases: whether sparsity would complement modularity and orthogonalization or conflict with architectural constraints that maintain task separation. This uncertainty is consequential because an intervention beneficial for one architecture (e.g., pruning shared backbones) could inadvertently remove degrees of freedom that specialized architectures rely upon to represent orthogonal task features, leading to severe representational degradation and performance loss if pruning is too aggressive or mismatched to architectural demands.

Actor–critic architectures present asymmetric sensitivity to capacity allocation: prior reports suggested critic scaling often yields large benefits, but it remained unexplored whether selectively reducing actor capacity via pruning could improve efficiency without harming critical value estimation. Without targeted experiments, practitioners lacked guidance on pruning granularity in continuous-control multi-task settings and whether selective sparsification could preserve or even enhance actor adaptability while leaving critic representational power intact. This question is important because naïvely pruning both actor and critic risks removing representational capacity where it is most needed.

Multi-task optimization improvements have been proposed via gradient projection methods (e.g., PCGrad) and via regularizers (weight decay), but it was unclear whether such techniques would be complementary to magnitude-based pruning schedules or whether interactions (e.g., weight shrinkage increasing candidates for pruning) would hamper the selective retention of useful parameters. Clarifying these interactions is necessary to design combined optimization pipelines that consistently improve multi-task learning, rather than relying on additive intuition that may fail due to subtle dynamics between optimizers and sparsification heuristics.

Understanding the temporal nature of how sparsification alters optimization dynamics is important because the timing and patterns of sensitivity and representational diversity affect both stability and the agent's continuing ability to learn new tasks. Prior literature demonstrated pruning can help single-task RL, but lacked a comparative view of how gradual magnitude schedules versus dynamic rewiring influence the evolution of curvature proxies and activation distributions over training in multi-task contexts. Without this knowledge, it is difficult to align a pruning strategy with desired adaptation properties (e.g., rapid early compression vs sustained exploratory rewiring).

The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis and rewinding-based sparse subnetworks have demonstrated promise in supervised and single-task settings by identifying trainable sparse subnets; however, multi-task learning imposes varied and possibly conflicting gradient signals and representational requirements, raising the question whether a single static sparse subnetwork discovered early can serve all tasks. Absent empirical comparison, it was unknown whether the LTH approach would transfer to MTRL or whether dynamic sparsification would be necessary to sustain plasticity across tasks.

Normalization layers are often proposed to stabilize training and mitigate covariate shift and have been linked to improved plasticity in some single-task studies; however, their global scaling and per-sample normalization effects could inadvertently homogenize feature activations across tasks, reducing task-specific representational distinctions necessary for multi-task learning. Without comparative empirical evidence, the trade-off between reduced dormancy and loss of effective representational dimensionality under LayerNorm in MTRL remained speculative.

Applying dynamic sparsification methods—Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP), which progressively increases layer-wise sparsity following a cubic schedule from a start time $t_{\text{start}}$ to an end time $t_{\text{end}}$ to reach a target sparsity $\rho_F$, and Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET), which maintains a fixed global sparsity $\rho$ while periodically pruning a fraction $\varepsilon$ of smallest-magnitude connections and regrowing the same number of new random connections—consistently modifies three correlative indicators of plasticity in multi-task agents trained on MiniGrid benchmarks (MT3, MT5, MT7): (a) the percentage of dormant neurons (fraction of neurons whose mean absolute activation normalized within the layer is below threshold $\tau$) is reduced under sparsification compared to dense baselines, with SET typically attaining the lowest dormancy levels across actor and critic components; (b) the effective rank of shared feature representations, measured as $\operatorname{srank}_\delta(\Phi)=\min_k\{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^k\sigma_i}{\sum_{i=1}^d\sigma_i}\ge 1-\delta\}$ for singular values $\sigma_i$ of feature matrix $\Phi$, is maintained or increased under sparsification relative to dense baselines (preventing representational collapse in many settings); and (c) the trace of the Fisher Information Matrix, $\operatorname{Tr}(F)=\mathbb{E}_{s,a\sim\pi}[\|\nabla_\theta\log\pi(a\mid s)\|_2^2]$, generally stabilizes at lower or less volatile values for sparse agents, with GMP often showing a peak‑and‑decline pattern and SET maintaining a low, steady trace.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that GMP and SET reduce plasticity-loss indicators in MTRL is the empirical anchor of the paper, but its credibility is constrained by two load-bearing measurement uncertainties. P1 raises the risk that the plasticity indicators are measured on a fixed replay buffer whose composition may not faithfully represent current network state across all tasks, especially as task sampling evolves; if this measurement methodology is flawed, the entire visual evidence for dormancy reduction, effective rank maintenance, and Fisher trace stabilization collapses. P2 highlights that the indicator differences are assessed qualitatively without statistical testing across 30 seeds, meaning the visible curve separations could be within noise. These two premises compound each other: an uncertain measurement applied without significance testing is doubly exposed. On the strength side, H1 provides substantial cross-architecture and cross-benchmark replication of the directional patterns (9 architecture-benchmark combinations), which partially offsets P1's measurement concern by showing that whatever quantity is being measured, it moves consistently under sparsification in many settings. H2 provides transparency via standard definitions, but this does not address the implementation-specific buffer and threshold choices raised in P1. Overall, the conclusion holds with moderate probability (~0.55): the consistency across many settings suggests the effect is real, but the measurement infrastructure is insufficiently validated and the lack of statistical testing leaves the magnitude and significance of the indicator changes unquantified.

nodes.title: Sparsification via GMP and SET reduces common plasticity‑loss indicators in MTRL

nodes.content: Across multiple MTRL architectures (shared-backbone MTPPO, Mixture-of-Experts MoE) and MiniGrid benchmarks (MT3, MT5, MT7), agents trained with GMP (final target sparsity $95\%$ in main experiments) or SET (fixed sparsity $95\%$ with ERK initialization and evolution parameter $\varepsilon$) achieve higher normalized interquantile mean (IQM) aggregate returns than their dense counterparts: for example, in the MTPPO configuration on MT5, GMP attains IQM = 0.81 (95% CI: 0.75–0.86) and SET attains IQM = 0.80 (95% CI: 0.75–0.84), both exceeding the dense IQM = 0.65 (95% CI: 0.61–0.71); similar improvements are observed in MoE results. These sparse agents also compare favorably against alternative plasticity interventions and common regularization baselines in many settings.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that sparse agents outperform dense baselines relies on performance comparisons (Table 1, Figure 1) that benefit from methodologically sound reporting (IQM with CIs, H3) and comprehensive coverage (three architectures, three benchmarks for each method, H4's relevance extends to this conclusion as well). However, P3's concern about asymmetric hyperparameter tuning is load-bearing: if the dense baseline is undertuned relative to sparse methods, the observed performance gap could be inflated. This is a comparative risk that would shift the conclusion from "sparse agents outperform" to "optimized sparse agents outperform a default dense baseline." P4 raises the limited generalization beyond MiniGrid-style environments, which is a boundary issue—the conclusion as stated does not claim generalization beyond the tested benchmarks, but practitioners may extrapolate. The dominant risk is P3, which is partially offset by the fact that the dense baselines are taken from prior work (Hendawy et al., 2024) with recognized hyperparameters, and the improvements are consistent across architectures where each architecture has its own baseline. Still, without a dedicated dense sweep, the danger remains. The performance layer is the strongest underwritten layer due to H3 (CIs enable direct assessment of significance) and H4's cross-architecture consistency. The conclusion holds with good probability (~0.70): the aggregate pattern is convincing, but the caveat about tuning asymmetry prevents a higher rating.

nodes.title: Sparse agents frequently outperform dense baselines in aggregated multi‑task performance

nodes.content: The effectiveness of Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP, which progressively increases sparsity following a cubic schedule) and Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET, which maintains constant sparsity with periodic pruning and regrowth) depends on architectural design: Multi-Task PPO (MTPPO) and Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures consistently benefit from dynamic sparsification with improved plasticity metrics (neuron dormancy—percentage of neurons whose normalized mean absolute activation is below a threshold $\tau$; effective rank—the minimum number $k$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i / \sum_{i=1}^d \sigma_i \ge 1-\delta$ for singular values $\sigma_i$ of the feature matrix; and Fisher trace—the expected squared gradient norm of the log-policy, $\operatorname{Tr}(F) = \mathbb{E}_{s,a\sim\pi}[\|\nabla_\theta \log \pi(a|s)\|_2^2]$) and higher aggregate returns, whereas Mixture of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE) exhibits more variable outcomes—SET sometimes reduces performance for MOORE despite lowering dormancy, and very aggressive pruning levels (e.g., GMP at 99% sparsity) can produce rank collapse in MOORE, evidenced by a sharp drop in effective rank accompanied by increased Fisher Trace and neuron dormancy, and corresponding late-training performance degradation.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion has two sub-claims: (a) sparsification benefits are architecture-dependent, and (b) extreme pruning can induce representational collapse. Claim (a) is well-supported by H4 (controlled three-architecture comparison) and the systematic evidence that SET reduces MOORE's performance while improving MTPPO/MoE. However, P6 raises the unresolved mechanistic question of why SET harms MOORE, meaning the architecture-dependence is descriptively established but not explained, which weakens its value for informing design choices. Claim (b) is supported by H5 (direct evidence of rank collapse in MOORE at 99% sparsity via effective rank, Fisher trace, and dormancy), but P5 limits the evidence to a single architecture at a single extreme sparsity level; it is unknown whether the collapse would occur in other architectures if tested at 99% sparsity. The two premises are partially offset by H4 and H5, but P5 is a serious generalization risk: the collapse could be a MOORE-specific artifact or a universal phenomenon; the evidence base is too narrow to distinguish. The prior probability of 0.65 reflects that the architecture-dependence claim is well-supported for the tested architectures and sparsities (0.80+), but the extreme collapse claim is preliminary and limited in scope (~0.5).

nodes.title: Sparsification benefits are architecture‑dependent and extreme pruning can induce representational collapse

nodes.content: In the continuous-control Multi-Task Multi-Headed Soft Actor-Critic (MTMH-SAC) experiments on MetaWorld MT10, applying Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) exclusively to the actor network (keeping the critic dense) yields a final mean success rate of 81% (95% CI: 0.77–0.83), outperforming the dense MTMH-SAC baseline (73%; 95% CI: 0.67–0.75) and global actor+critic pruning (75%; 95% CI: 0.73–0.78). Actor-only pruning also sustained reduced actor neuron dormancy (percentage of neurons with normalized mean absolute activation below a threshold $\tau$) and increased mean effective rank (dimensionality of feature space measured via singular values) compared to both the dense and globally pruned agents, indicating a role-dependent benefit of targeted sparsification in actor–critic settings.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion is supported by a well-designed experimental contrast (H5: three-condition design isolating actor pruning) and is mechanistically reinforced by actor plasticity metrics. However, the evidence base is narrow: P7 notes that the experiment uses only a single continuous-control benchmark (MT10) with only 10 seeds, limiting statistical power and generalization. P8 highlights that the plasticity improvement claim rests on only two of three indicators (dormancy and effective rank; Fisher trace is volatile), so the mechanistic corroboration is partial. The three-condition design (H5) partially offsets P8 by providing a strong causal contrast for performance, but it does not fully compensate for the small number of seeds and single benchmark. The dominant risk is generalization: practitioners need to know whether this selectivity benefit holds across other continuous-control domains. The layer of unreliability is the generalization/extrapolation scope, while the qualitative direction and quantitative magnitude (81% vs 73%) are underwritten by H5's controlled comparison and H8? Actually H8 is for conclusion 8; H5 is for conclusion 4. The conclusion's prior probability of 0.50 reflects that the internal validity of the experiment is good, but the external validity is very limited; the conclusion as stated implies broader applicability than the evidence covers.

nodes.title: Selective actor pruning in continuous control improves MetaWorld MT10 success rates and actor plasticity

nodes.content: In Multi-Task PPO (MTPPO) experiments on the MT5 benchmark, Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) in isolation achieves the highest final aggregated returns; pairing GMP with Weight Decay (GMP+WD) or PCGrad (gradient surgery that projects conflicting gradients to reduce interference) yields no additional performance gains and in some cases slightly worsens plasticity indicators and final returns. PCGrad by itself improves over a dense baseline, but the combination GMP+PCGrad does not surpass GMP alone; GMP+WD exhibits plasticity dynamics similar to GMP with minor degradations in some metrics, consistent with the notion that weight decay can increase the pool of small-magnitude weights that magnitude-based pruning may subsequently remove.

metadata.narrative: The claim that GMP+WD and GMP+PCGrad yield no additive benefit is based on a single architecture+benchmark (MTPPO, MT5), raising a strong generalization risk (P9). Additionally, P10 highlights the lack of joint hyperparameter search for the combined treatments, so the null result may be specific to the tested coefficient values. H6 provides a comprehensive reporting of both performance and plasticity indicators, which is a strength in showing that the combinations do not improve plasticity dynamics either, ruling out the alternative where they might improve performance through different mechanisms. However, H6 does not offset P9 or P10 because it only characterizes the dynamics under the tested (potentially suboptimal) combined hyperparameters. The failure modes of both premises are concrete: if GMP+PCGrad were beneficial on MoE (untested), or if tuning WD coefficient differently in combination with GMP yielded synergy, the conclusion would be false for those settings. The prior probability of 0.40 is low because the negative result is severely under-tested; the paper's own caveats about hyperparameter sensitivity reinforce this. The conclusion survives as a specific finding for MTPPO/MT5 with the tested hyperparameters, but not as a general claim about interaction.

nodes.title: Combining GMP with Weight Decay or PCGrad yields no consistent additive benefit over GMP alone

nodes.content: Although both Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) and Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) improve correlative plasticity indicators (neuron dormancy—percentage of neurons with normalized mean absolute activation below threshold $\tau$; effective rank—dimensionality of feature space via singular values; Fisher trace—$\operatorname{Tr}(F)=\mathbb{E}_{s,a\sim\pi}[\|\nabla_\theta\log\pi(a|s)\|_2^2]$) relative to dense baselines, they produce different temporal patterns: GMP commonly exhibits a characteristic peak‑and‑decline in the Fisher trace (indicative of transiently increased sensitivity followed by convergence to flatter minima) and tends to reduce dormancy more strongly in actor than critic in some settings, whereas SET produces consistently low Fisher trace values and maintains very low neuron dormancy throughout training due to its continual rewiring; these distinct dynamics imply differing adaptation profiles—GMP promotes staged sparsification adaptation while SET supports continuous topological exploration.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion asserts empirical distinctness between GMP's and SET's plasticity dynamics and links those dynamics to different adaptation profiles. The empirical distinctness is supported by cross-architecture replication (H7), which shows that the GMP peak-and-decline and SET stable-low Fisher trace patterns appear across multiple architectures and benchmarks. However, P11 notes that all descriptions are qualitative (no quantified measures of peak, duration, variance), and P12 highlights that the claimed link to adaptation profiles is untested (no direct adaptation experiments). These two premises interact: even if the patterns are real, their interpretation as informing adaptation profiles is speculative. H7 provides evidence that the patterns are reproducible, but this only addresses the descriptive part of the conclusion, not the interpretive part. The conclusion's prior probability is low (0.35) because the dynamic patterns themselves are described qualitatively (P11), and the adaptation profile link is pure speculation (P12). The conclusion contributes an observation but not a validated insight; it is more a hypothesis-generation step than an established finding.

nodes.title: GMP and SET induce distinct plasticity dynamics (GMP peak‑and‑decline vs SET stable low sensitivity) informing different adaptation profiles

nodes.content: Preliminary experiments on the MT5 benchmark (a multi-task MiniGrid crossing of 5 tasks) show that Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) style rewinding (early rewinding at iteration 1 with 1 epoch warmup to target sparsity 95%) did not produce significant improvements over single-task baselines and underperformed relative to Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) and Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) in multi-task scenarios, indicating that fixed sparse subnetworks found via early rewinding are less capable of adapting across diverse tasks compared to dynamically adapting sparsification strategies.

metadata.narrative: This conclusion is based on a single preliminary experiment with one LTH configuration (early rewinding, one architecture, one benchmark), as highlighted by P13. The paper's own framing as "preliminary" signals that the evidence is not intended to be definitive, but the conclusion statement does not clearly reserve judgment. There are no highlights that strengthen this conclusion—no systematic tuning, no multi-architecture replication. The dominant risk is that LTH might be competitive under different rewinding schemes (later rewinding, multi-iteration, different sparsity levels), as P13 details. The prior probability of 0.20 reflects that the conclusion is weakly supported and likely specific to the tested configuration; a more thorough comparison could easily overturn it. The narrative notes that the conclusion should be read as a preliminary observation rather than a reliable finding.

nodes.title: Lottery‑Ticket style rewinding underperforms GMP and SET in multi‑task settings

nodes.content: Layer Normalization (LayerNorm) applied in the evaluated multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) settings tends to produce very low dormant neuron percentages (neurons with normalized mean absolute activation below threshold $\tau$) but simultaneously causes a severe and persistent reduction in effective rank (dimensionality of feature space measured via singular values) of feature representations, correlating with substantially worse aggregated multi-task returns compared to both dense and sparsified agents; this indicates that normalization can suppress neuron inactivity at the cost of representational diversity in multi-task contexts.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that LayerNorm reduces dormancy but collapses rank and harms performance is supported by a consistent empirical pattern across three architectures and three benchmarks (H8 shows the trade-off and the poor performance). However, two load-bearing uncertainties undermine its generality. P14 raises the concern that the severe rank collapse may be specific to LayerNorm's placement in this implementation; without reporting placement details, other implementations might avoid the collapse. P15 challenges the causal interpretation: the paper claims the rank collapse causes poor performance, but alternative mechanisms (e.g., optimization instability, small gradient norms) could explain both the low rank and the poor performance, making the rank collapse an epiphenomenon. H8 only shows correlation, not causation. The prior probability of 0.40 reflects that the empirical observation of collapse+ poor performance is robust within the paper's specific implementation, but both the generality across implementations and the causal interpretation are insufficiently supported. The conclusion's practical utility is limited because the negative result is not causally explained and the implementation details are missing.

nodes.title: Layer Normalization reduces dormancy but collapses representational rank, harming multi‑task performance

nodes.content:
In multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) agents with Multi-Task PPO (MTPPO), Mixture of Experts (MoE), or Mixture of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE) architectures trained on MiniGrid benchmarks (MT3, MT5, MT7), the three plasticity indicators are computed as follows: neuron dormancy is the percentage of neurons whose normalized mean absolute activation is below threshold $\tau=0.001$, measured on a plasticity replay buffer with up to 100,000 observations sampled with replacement; effective rank is $\operatorname{srank}_\delta(\Phi)=\min_k\{(\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i)/(\sum_{i=1}^d \sigma_i) \ge 1-\delta\}$ for singular values $\sigma_i$ of the shared feature extractor, where $\delta$ is unspecified; and Fisher trace is $\operatorname{Tr}(F)=\mathbb{E}_{s,a\sim\pi}[\|\nabla_\theta \log \pi(a|s)\|_2^2]$ with a batch size of 1024. These computations rely on a single fixed-size buffer whose composition may be dominated by early-task experiences when tasks are sampled uniformly per episode.Fig. 2; Fig. 17; Fig. 20
      C.1, C.2, C.3 in appendix

metadata.failure_mode: If the replay buffer's composition becomes biased toward early tasks or high-return episodes, the measured dormant percentage, effective rank, and Fisher trace may incorrectly attribute indicator changes to sparsification when they actually reflect buffer staleness: a drop in dormant percentage could occur because the buffer no longer contains diverse task observations, not because the network's activations have genuinely become less dormant. Since the conclusion's entire support rests on these indicator trajectories, their invalidation would remove the quantitative evidence that sparsity reduces plasticity-loss indicators in MTRL, leaving only qualitative visual trends without a reliable measurement basis.
metadata.weakness_reason: The measurement protocol uses a single replay buffer of fixed size (100,000) to approximate expectations for all three indicators; as task sampling is random with replacement, the buffer's content may become imbalanced toward tasks seen more frequently early in training or toward episodes with high returns, biasing the computed metrics away from representing the current plasticity state across the entire multi-task distribution. The effective rank definition requires a tolerance δ but δ is not reported, making the metric's sensitivity to arbitrary cutoffs unknown and preventing reproducibility of the exact numeric values shown in the figures. The dormant threshold τ=0.001 was used without evidence that this value meaningfully separates truly inactive neurons from low-activity but useful ones in the multi-task setting.

nodes.title: Plasticity indicator measurement fidelity

nodes.content: For the plasticity indicators (dormant neuron percentage, effective rank, Fisher trace) between Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP), Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET), and dense baselines on MiniGrid benchmarks (MT3, MT5, MT7), differences are assessed solely by visual inspection of overlaid learning curves, without any formal statistical hypothesis test (e.g., t-test, permutation test, bootstrap test of difference at final epoch or across training trajectories) that would quantify the probability that observed differences are due to chance across the 30 random seeds used.

metadata.failure_mode: If the observed differences in plasticity indicators are merely noise fluctuations (i.e., overlapping seed-level distributions), then the conclusion that GMP and SET reduce plasticity-loss indicators would be unsupported. The entire argument that sparsification improves plasticity in MTRL would lose its quantitative grounding, leaving only performance improvements (Conclusion 2) without a mechanistic or correlative explanation, which would reduce the paper's contribution to a performance comparison without identified mediators.
metadata.weakness_reason: With 30 seeds per condition, the plasticity indicator curves show considerable seed-to-seed variance (as seen in confidence intervals of performance, though not displayed for plasticity metrics in the same way — the plasticity metric curves appear to be means without error bars). Without a statistical test, claims that one method "reduces" dormancy or "maintains higher effective rank" are based on visual interpretation of the curve separation, which may be influenced by outlier seeds or overlapping distributions. The field standard for claiming a difference in RL metrics involves either reporting confidence intervals (as done for performance IQM) or performing a paired comparison across seeds at final or multiple evaluation points. The absence of this for plasticity indicators weakens the evidential basis for asserting that sparsification consistently and significantly alters these metrics relative to dense baselines.

nodes.title: No statistical testing of indicator differences

nodes.content: In the comparison of sparse agents (Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) at 95% sparsity, Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) at 95% sparsity) against dense baselines on MiniGrid MT3, MT5, and MT7 benchmarks using Multi-Task PPO (MTPPO), Mixture of Experts (MoE), and Mixture of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE) architectures, the dense baseline hyperparameters (learning rate $1\times10^{-3}$ for both actor and critic, hidden size 128, number of linear layers $2\times|\mathcal{T}|$ where $|\mathcal{T}|$ is the number of tasks) were adopted from a prior work (Hendawy et al., 2024) without a dedicated hyperparameter sweep for the dense configuration equivalent to the sweeps performed for GMP (pruning window, frequency, target sparsity) and SET (evolution parameter $\varepsilon$, sparsity distribution parameter $\zeta$, evolution frequency), introducing the possibility that an alternative dense hyperparameter setting could yield higher Interquantile Mean (IQM) and narrow the performance gap claimed against sparse methods.

metadata.failure_mode: If an undertuned dense baseline is compared to a carefully tuned sparse agent, the reported IQM advantage (e.g., MT5 MTPPO: dense 0.65 vs GMP 0.81) could shrink or vanish when dense hyperparameters are optimized. The conclusion that sparsification improves aggregated multi-task performance would then be contingent on a particular tuning regime and would not support a general claim of sparsity-driven improvement; it would reduce to "a specific tuned sparse configuration outperforms a specific untuned dense configuration," which is weaker and less useful for practitioners.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper demonstrates extensive tuning for GMP (Figure 8) and SET (Figure 9) on the MT5 MTPPO configuration, including sweeps over pruning window, frequency, target sparsity for GMP, and evolution percentage, sparsity distribution, and evolution frequency for SET. For the dense baseline, no such systematic tuning is reported; the chosen hyperparameters are "largely adopted from Hendawy et al. (2024)" (Appendix A). If the dense baseline were undertuned relative to the sparse methods, the observed performance advantage could partly reflect optimization effort rather than a fundamental benefit of sparsity, weakening the conclusion that sparse agents "frequently outperform dense baselines." The paper acknowledges this possibility indirectly by noting that dense models are "overparameterized" but does not control for tuning asymmetry.

nodes.title: Potential asymmetric hyperparameter tuning of dense baselines

nodes.content: The performance improvements of Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) and Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) over dense baselines are measured only on two families of environments: MiniGrid benchmarks (MT3, MT5, MT7) which are partially observable grid-world Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) with discrete actions and sparse rewards, and MetaWorld MT10 (for actor-only pruning in continuous control). These settings do not include visual observations (image-based state spaces with pixel-level distractors), high-dimensional continuous state spaces with contact dynamics (e.g., robotic manipulation with force feedback), or task distributions with more than 10 tasks. Therefore, there is no evidence that sparsification benefits generalize beyond these specific POMDP settings.

metadata.failure_mode: If the performance gains are specific to MiniGrid-style environments (sparse reward, small grid world, partial observability with limited visual complexity), then practitioners working with image-based or contact-rich continuous-control tasks cannot rely on the paper's conclusion that sparsification improves MTRL performance. The conclusion's utility would be restricted to a narrow regime, materially narrowing its claimed scope unless the authors explicitly bound it.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper explicitly acknowledges "generalization beyond the evaluated benchmarks (different observational modalities, larger task suites, longer training horizons)" as future work in its open questions. The claim that sparse agents "frequently outperform dense baselines" is stated without an explicit scope restriction to the tested environments. Since the MTRL community uses a wide variety of benchmarks (e.g., Atari-based multi-task, MetaWorld ML1/ML45, DM Control suites, CARLA multi-task), the absence of evidence from these domains means the conclusion may not hold for many practically relevant MTRL settings. This is a standard limitation but a load-bearing one for practitioners deciding whether to adopt sparsification.

nodes.title: Limited generalization of performance gains to other benchmarks

nodes.content: In the Mixture of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE) architecture on the MT5 benchmark (5-task MiniGrid), the observation that extreme pruning induces representational collapse—evidenced by a sharp drop in effective rank (dimensionality of feature space via singular values), increased Fisher trace ($\operatorname{Tr}(F)=\mathbb{E}_{s,a\sim\pi}[\|\nabla_\theta \log \pi(a|s)\|_2^2]$), and increased neuron dormancy (percentage of neurons with normalized mean absolute activation below a threshold $\tau$) around epoch 125—is reported for Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) at a target sparsity of 99% using a cubic schedule, but is not demonstrated for other sparsity levels (95%, 80%) in MOORE, for other architectures (Multi-Task PPO (MTPPO), Mixture of Experts (MoE)) at 99% sparsity, or for Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) at any sparsity level. The root cause of the collapse (whether due to the increased sparsity itself, the aggressive cubic schedule at high pruning ratios, optimization instability triggered by the pruning events, or an interaction with MOORE's orthogonality constraint) is not isolated.

metadata.failure_mode: If the rank collapse at 99% sparsity is a generic phenomenon that would also occur in MTPPO and MoE at 99% sparsity (which were not tested), then the conclusion that sparsification benefits are architecture-dependent because MOORE exhibits collapse would be an artifact of incomplete testing: the collapse might be universal at 99% sparsity, and MOORE simply happened to be the only architecture tested at that level. Conversely, if the collapse is due to a specific interaction with MOORE's orthogonalization that is not fundamental to pruning, then the conclusion that extreme pruning can induce collapse in MOORE is correct but the broader message about architecture-dependence could be misattributed to sparsification-pruning interactions rather than to MOORE's unique design.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper presents the rank collapse as a key cautionary finding for practitioners, but the evidence rests on a single architecture at a single extreme sparsity level. The authors note in Appendix H that "99% sparsity leads to performance degradation later in training" and correlates with rank collapse. However, without demonstrating whether the collapse occurs in other architectures when pruned to 99%, it is impossible to attribute the collapse to architecture-specific properties (e.g., orthogonality constraints reducing degrees of freedom) versus a generic consequence of extreme pruning that only becomes visible in MOORE because it already operates near capacity. The causal mechanism remains correlational, as the paper does not manipulate potential confounders (learning rate, pruning frequency, schedule shape) to see if the collapse can be triggered or prevented.

nodes.title: Rank collapse evidence is limited to MOORE at 99% sparsity only

nodes.content: In the Mixture of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE) architecture on the MT5 benchmark (5-task MiniGrid), Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) at fixed 95% sparsity achieves an Interquantile Mean (IQM) of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.72–0.83) compared to dense MOORE at 0.84 (95% CI: 0.81–0.85), representing a statistically non-overlapping performance decline. SET reduces neuron dormancy in MOORE, but no mechanistic explanation is provided for why reduced dormancy (percentage of neurons with normalized mean absolute activation below a threshold $\tau$) does not translate into improved performance—whether due to interference with the orthogonality regularization, random regrowth disrupting task-specific expert subspaces, or some other factor—leaving the negative result unexplained and potentially due to poor SET hyperparameter choices specific to MOORE.

metadata.failure_mode: If the performance decline of SET in MOORE is due to suboptimal hyperparameters (e.g., regrowth frequency too high for MOORE's orthogonality maintenance), then the conclusion that sparsification benefits are architecture-dependent would be an overgeneralization from a non-optimized configuration: a properly tuned SET might match dense MOORE performance, making the architecture-dependence claim weaker. Conversely, if the decline is intrinsic, the absence of mechanistic understanding means the conclusion provides no actionable insight for designing sparsification-compatible architectures.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper acknowledges that "these specific plasticity modulations, such as SET's reduced dormancy in MOORE, generally did not translate into performance improvements for this architecture, with SET often resulting in a slight performance decline." This is an important but uninterpreted result. Without analysis of whether SET's random regrowth disrupts the orthogonalization that MOORE relies upon for task separation, or whether the reduced plasticity indicators are actually detrimental rather than beneficial in a model with built-in interference prevention, the conclusion that sparsification benefits are architecture-dependent remains descriptive rather than explanatory. Practitioners cannot infer from this whether to avoid SET with MOORE entirely or to adjust SET hyperparameters (e.g., reduce regrowth magnitude, preserve orthogonal structures).

nodes.title: SET's performance decline in MOORE is not explained mechanistically

nodes.content: Actor-only Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) at 95% sparsity on MetaWorld MT10 achieves a final mean success rate of 81% (95% CI: 0.77–0.83), compared to a dense Multi-Task Multi-Headed Soft Actor-Critic (MTMH-SAC) baseline of 73% (95% CI: 0.67–0.75) and global actor+critic pruning of 75% (95% CI: 0.73–0.78), based on a single continuous-control benchmark with 10 random seeds per condition. No replication is available on other continuous-control benchmarks (e.g., MetaWorld ML45, DM Control, Robosuite) or with alternative actor-critic algorithms (e.g., TD3, D4PG, PPO continuous).

metadata.failure_mode: If the selective actor-pruning benefit does not replicate on other continuous-control benchmarks (e.g., due to different task structures, reward scales, or observation spaces), the conclusion that actor-only pruning improves multi-task continuous control success rates would be limited to the specific MT10/MTMH-SAC combination, substantially reducing its generality for practitioners. The paper's claim that this finding "extends our MiniGrid-based plasticity findings to the more complex MetaWorld benchmark" would be valid only for that single extension point.
metadata.weakness_reason: With 10 seeds, the confidence intervals for success rates are wider than the 30-seed MiniGrid experiments, but the reported intervals for the three conditions do not overlap, giving modest confidence in the ordering. However, the experiment captures only one continuous-control setting (MT10, 10 tasks, SAC). The claim that selective actor pruning is beneficial in continuous control rests entirely on this single experiment. Alternative benchmarks differ in action dimension, observation type (e.g., pixel-based vs. state-based), reward density, and number of tasks, all of which could modulate the effect. The paper acknowledges the need for "generalization beyond the evaluated benchmarks" as future work, but the conclusion as stated does not restrict its scope to the MT10 setting.

nodes.title: Selective actor pruning results are based on single benchmark with 10 seeds

nodes.content: In the MetaWorld MT10 experiments with actor-only Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP), the claim that selective pruning improves actor plasticity is supported by a reduction in actor dormant neurons (percentage of neurons with normalized mean absolute activation below threshold $\tau$) and an increase in mean effective rank (dimensionality of feature space via singular values); however, the Fisher trace ($\operatorname{Tr}(F)=\mathbb{E}_{s,a\sim\pi}[\|\nabla_\theta \log \pi(a|s)\|_2^2]$) remains highly volatile for all methods and shows no discernible pattern. Two of the three plasticity indicators—dormancy and effective rank—point in the direction of improvement, while the third (Fisher trace) shows no consistent difference.

metadata.failure_mode: If the Fisher trace is genuinely unchanged by actor-only pruning in continuous control, then the notion that sparsification leads to convergence to flatter minima (a core interpretive theme in the paper's Section 6) is not supported in this setting. The conclusion of improved actor plasticity would then rest only on dormancy and effective rank, which are arguably weaker proxies for learning capacity than the combined evidence across three indicators presented in the MiniGrid experiments. This reduces the strength of the conclusion from a consistent pattern to a tentative one, potentially misleading practitioners who rely on plasticity indicators as a whole.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper treats plasticity as a multi-indicator concept (dormancy, effective rank, Fisher trace) and in the MiniGrid experiments all three indicators generally improve under sparsification. In the MetaWorld continuous-control case, one of the three indicators (Fisher trace) does not differentiate between conditions. The conclusion that plasticity is improved therefore relies on a subset of the indicators, weakening the consistency of the evidence. It is possible that the Fisher trace's volatility and lack of pattern reflect that the actor's Fisher information is not a meaningful plasticity metric in continuous control with stochastic policies (SAC uses Gaussian policy with state-dependent variance), or that the pruning does not affect the curvature of the loss surface in the same way as in discrete-action PPO. Without clarifying why the Fisher trace behaves differently, the claim of improved actor plasticity is only partially supported.

nodes.title: Actor plasticity improvement under selective pruning is based on two of three indicators

nodes.content: The combination of Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) with Weight Decay (WD) or PCGrad (gradient surgery method that projects conflicting gradients) provides no consistent additive benefit over GMP alone in experiments on the Multi-Task PPO (MTPPO) architecture with the MT5 benchmark (5-task MiniGrid, 30 seeds). No combination tests are performed on Mixture of Experts (MoE) or Mixture of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE) architectures, on other benchmarks (MT3, MT7), or on the MetaWorld continuous-control setup. Therefore, the conclusion is specific to shared-backbone MTPPO on MT5.

metadata.failure_mode: If GMP+WD or GMP+PCGrad were to produce additive benefits on MoE or MOORE architectures, the conclusion that they yield no consistent additive benefit would be incorrect for those architectures, and practitioners using those architectures would be misled into not trying these combinations. The paper's claim that the result suggests "GMP's inherent regularization effects and capacity optimization" are not enhanced by these optimizers would be architecture-specific, not general.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper explores interactions with optimizers only on one setting to keep the experimental scope manageable, but the conclusion is stated as a general finding ("yields no consistent additive benefit over GMP alone"). The choice of MTPPO and MT5 is reasonable for an ablation, but without evidence from at least one other architecture or benchmark, it is unknown whether the lack of synergy is a general property or a peculiarity of that architecture. For example, PCGrad might be more beneficial with MoE where gradient conflicts across experts are more pronounced, or weight decay might help SET (which was not tested) due to different dynamics. The paper's own open questions note hyperparameter sensitivity as an unresolved issue, which further limits confidence in the generality of the null result.

nodes.title: Combination tests limited to one architecture and one benchmark

nodes.content: In the GMP+WD and GMP+PCGrad experiments on Multi-Task PPO (MTPPO) with the MT5 benchmark (5-task MiniGrid), the hyperparameters for weight decay ($\lambda=1\times10^{-6}$) and PCGrad (default implementation from Yu et al., 2020) were carried over from the single-method sweeps without a dedicated joint hyperparameter search for the combined treatment. GMP+WD exhibits plasticity dynamics similar to GMP alone with minor degradations, and GMP+PCGrad does not surpass GMP alone.

metadata.failure_mode: If a different weight decay coefficient or a different pruning schedule for GMP+WD yields additive benefits, then the conclusion that the combination yields no benefit would be refuted for those alternative hyperparameters. The paper's recommendation that GMP alone is sufficient would then be specific to the tested hyperparameters and not a general design principle. Since the paper does not bound this conclusion by explicitly stating "under the hyperparameters tested," it may be misinterpreted as a definitive negative result.
metadata.weakness_reason: The weight decay coefficient (1e-6) was tuned for WD alone (Figure 12 shows that 1e-6 performed best among tested values), but when combined with GMP, the optimal λ may differ because GMP already removes small-magnitude weights, so WD's effect on remaining weights could become detrimental at the previously optimal λ. Similarly, PCGrad's gradient projection may interact with GMP's masking in ways that require different scaling or learning rates. By not searching the joint space, the paper may have missed combined configurations where synergy exists. The claim of "no consistent additive benefit" is therefore a claim about the particular hyperparameter configurations tested, not about the interaction in principle. The authors acknowledge that weight decay "could lead to a less discerning pruning process," which suggests they are aware of potential harmful interactions, but they did not test whether adjusting the pruning schedule or weight decay strength could mitigate this.

nodes.title: Potential suboptimal combined hyperparameters

nodes.content: In Multi-Task PPO (MTPPO) and Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures on the MT5 benchmark (5-task MiniGrid), and similar patterns are observed on MT3 and MT7, Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) exhibits a "peak-and-decline" pattern in the Fisher trace (a transient increase followed by a decrease toward low values) while Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) maintains a "low, stable" Fisher trace throughout training. These dynamics are described qualitatively based on visual inspection of learning curves, without quantitative metrics such as peak magnitude, timing of peak, post-peak stabilization value, variance across seeds, or statistical testing of the difference between GMP and SET curves.

metadata.failure_mode: If the visual differences are not statistically significant across seeds, then the claimed distinct dynamics would not exist, and the conclusion that GMP and SET produce different plasticity dynamics would be unsupported. The paper's interpretive discussion (Section 6) about GMP converging to flatter minima via peak-and-decline and SET maintaining robust optimization via low stable trace would lose its empirical foundation, reducing the paper's mechanistic contribution to speculation.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper distinguishes the two methods' plasticity dynamics as a key insight, but the characterization is entirely qualitative. Without reporting, e.g., the average Fisher trace at epochs 50-100 vs 150-200 with confidence intervals, or performing a functional data analysis to detect the peak, the claim that the patterns are distinct and reproducible rests on visual interpretation. The Fisher trace curves in Figure 2 appear to have no error bands (unlike the performance IQM curves), so seed-level variability is unknown. It is possible that GMP's "peak" is within the noise range of the measurement or that SET's trace also shows small peaks on a compressed scale. The absence of quantitative rigor weakens the strength of the conclusion that these patterns are real and inform "different adaptation profiles."

nodes.title: Distinct dynamics are described qualitatively without quantitative characterization

nodes.content: The distinct Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) peak-and-decline and Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) stable low Fisher trace dynamics are claimed to imply differing adaptation profiles—GMP promotes staged sparsification adaptation while SET supports continuous topological exploration. However, no experiment directly tests adaptation (e.g., measuring performance on new or held-out tasks after training, evaluating sample efficiency on previously seen tasks, or perturbing the policy and measuring recovery speed) that would validate whether these dynamics translate into different adaptation capabilities.

metadata.failure_mode: If the distinct Fisher dynamics do not translate into differential adaptation capabilities (e.g., if in a held-out task evaluation GMP and SET show similar adaptation profiles), then the conclusion that the dynamics inform different adaptation profiles would be incorrect: the dynamics would be epiphenomenal rather than predictive. The paper's contribution regarding the dynamics would then be limited to a descriptive observation without functional significance, weakening the conclusion's claim to provide insight into "how sparsification alters optimization dynamics" (as stated in the conclusion's problem statement).
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's Section 6 (Considerations) frames the Fisher trace as a proxy for curvature and links the peak-and-decline pattern to convergence to flatter minima, which is standard reasoning in optimization literature. However, the paper does not test whether GMP agents actually adapt better to new tasks or recover more quickly from distribution shift than SET agents; the adaptation claim is an extrapolation from the indicator pattern. Since the paper's earlier conclusion 5 already shows that GMP and SET have comparable final performance on MT5 (GMP IQM 0.81 vs SET 0.80 with overlapping CIs), the differences in plasticity dynamics do not correspond to a measurable difference in final aggregate performance, raising the question of whether the claimed different adaptation profiles have any practical consequence.

nodes.title: The link between distinct Fisher dynamics and adaptation profiles is not empirically tested

nodes.content: The comparison of Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) rewinding against Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) and Sparse Evolutionary Training (SET) on the MT5 benchmark (5-task MiniGrid) with Multi-Task PPO (MTPPO) uses a single LTH configuration: early rewinding at iteration 1, with the dense model pretrained for 1 epoch (the "warmup" typical of LTH), followed by pruning to the target sparsity (presumably 95% for consistency) and retraining. No search over rewinding points (e.g., after 10%, 25%, 50% of training), sparsity levels other than 95%, multiple rewinding iterations, or different architectures (Mixture of Experts (MoE), Mixture of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE)) is reported.

metadata.failure_mode: If a differently configured LTH (e.g., later rewinding, different sparsity, iterative rewinding) were to match or exceed GMP and SET performance in MTRL, then the conclusion that LTH underperforms relative to dynamic sparsification would be refuted for those configurations. The paper's assertion that fixed sparse subnetworks are "less capable of adapting across diverse tasks" would be undermined, as it would be specific to the early-rewinding variant tested. Practitioners might wrongly dismiss LTH as a viable MTRL strategy based on this single comparison.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper explicitly states "preliminary experiments on the MT5 benchmark" and Figure 1 shows LTH performing similarly to single-task baselines and below GMP and SET. However, the LTH literature demonstrates that rewinding to a very early iteration (e.g., at initialization or after very few steps) is often suboptimal; more effective LTH implementations rewind to a later iteration (e.g., at the sparsity convergence point). By using only one rewinding strategy, the paper may have underestimated LTH's potential in the multi-task setting. Additionally, LTH was originally designed for supervised classification, not RL, so its application to PPO may require adaptations (e.g., handling of off-policy data or value function loss) that were not explored. The paper acknowledges this limitation implicitly by using the term "preliminary," but the conclusion asserts that LTH underperforms GMP and SET in "multi-task settings" without reserving judgment until more exhaustive comparisons are made.

nodes.title: LTH comparison is preliminary with a single hyperparameter configuration

nodes.content: In multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) experiments (Multi-Task PPO (MTPPO), Mixture of Experts (MoE), Mixture of Orthogonal Experts (MOORE) on MiniGrid benchmarks MT3, MT5, MT7), Layer Normalization (LayerNorm) is applied to the hidden layers, though the exact placement (pre-activation vs post-activation) is unspecified. Under this implementation, LayerNorm reduces the effective rank (dimensionality of feature space via singular values) of the shared feature extractor to near-1 values rapidly and persistently, while also dramatically reducing dormant neuron percentages (neurons with normalized mean absolute activation below a threshold $\tau$). It is unknown whether different placement (pre-activation vs post-activation, convolutional layers vs linear layers, adding learnable parameters with gain/bias resetting) or different normalization variants (e.g., RMSNorm, LayerNorm without bias) would produce a different trade-off between dormancy and rank, potentially avoiding the performance harm.

metadata.failure_mode: If a different LayerNorm placement (e.g., after activation, or applied only to the critic, or with task-specific affine parameters) avoids the rank collapse while maintaining low dormancy and improves performance, then the conclusion that LayerNorm harms multi-task performance via rank collapse would be specific to the paper's implementation and not a general property. Practitioners who avoid LayerNorm in MTRL based on this paper may miss a beneficial configuration. The paper's strong recommendation against LayerNorm would be overbroad.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper criticizes LayerNorm for collapsing rank, but LayerNorm's implementation details are crucial for reproducibility and for understanding the mechanism. Standard LayerNorm normalizes across the feature dimension and then applies a learnable scale and shift. The paper does not report whether the normalization is applied to the feature extractor (conv layers + linear layers) or only to the MLP heads, whether it includes the learnable parameters, and whether the normalization is applied pre- or post-activation. These details affect whether the normalization can "undo" task-specific feature differentiation. Furthermore, in the multi-task setting, using a shared encoder with LayerNorm that enforces similar activation statistics across all tasks might be particularly harmful if tasks require very different feature distributions; but alternative placements (e.g., task-specific normalization) might mitigate this. Without implementation specifics, the conclusion that LayerNorm is detrimental in MTRL may be true only for the particular implementation choice, not for LayerNorm as a general mechanism.

nodes.title: LayerNorm's severe rank collapse may be implementation-specific

nodes.content: Layer Normalization (LayerNorm) produces low effective rank and low multi-task performance across all architectures and benchmarks, with Interquantile Mean (IQM) values ranging from 0.28 to 0.66 for LayerNorm compared to 0.65 to 0.87 for dense agents. This is interpreted as evidence that normalization "can suppress neuron inactivity at the cost of representational diversity," implying that the rank collapse causes the performance degradation. However, no causal mediation analysis or intervention (e.g., artificially increasing rank while keeping dormancy low, or applying regularization to maintain rank under LayerNorm) is conducted to confirm that the collapsed rank is a cause rather than a consequence of poor optimization.

metadata.failure_mode: If the poor performance under LayerNorm is primarily due to other optimization issues (e.g., increased gradient variance, reduced effective learning rate, or instability with PPO), and the rank collapse is a harmless epiphenomenon, then the conclusion that rank collapse harms performance would be incorrect. The juxtaposition of LayerNorm's low rank and low performance would not support the claim that representational collapse is the cause, and the paper's implication that interventions preserving rank while controlling dormancy (like sparsification) are superior because they avoid rank collapse would be weakened. The caution against normalization in MTRL would then be based on a misinterpreted correlation.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's claim about rank collapse harming performance is correlational. It is plausible that LayerNorm induces other optimization difficulties (e.g., small gradient magnitudes due to scale invariance, increased effective learning rate due to normalized activations, or reduced expressive capacity of the network through normalization's centering) that independently cause poor performance and also manifest as low effective rank. The paper does not disentangle these possibilities. The conclusion states that LayerNorm reduces dormancy but "collapses representational rank, harming multi-task performance," which assumes that the rank collapse is the (or a) mediating mechanism. Without causal evidence, this remains a hypothesis. The paper's Section 5.2 offers a plausible explanation (inadvertent gradient correlation across tasks) but does not test it.

nodes.title: Causal direction between rank collapse and poor performance is not established

nodes.content: Across three distinct multi-task architectures (MTPPO, MoE, MOORE) and three MiniGrid benchmarks (MT3, MT5, MT7), the plasticity indicator trajectories for GMP and SET relative to dense baselines show consistent directional patterns: GMP and SET reduce dormant neuron percentages (in both actor and critic), maintain or increase effective rank, and stabilize Fisher trace at lower values than dense networks, as shown in Figures 2, 4, 5, and the full set of appendix figures (Figures 16-21).

metadata.credit: This consistency across multiple architectures and benchmarks guards against the failure mode where a pattern observed in one architecture or benchmark is an artifact of that specific design or environment. The replication of the directional effects (reduced dormancy, maintained/increased effective rank, lower Fisher trace) in 9 architecture-benchmark combinations for both GMP and SET substantially increases the probability that these patterns reflect a genuine process linking sparsification to plasticity indicator changes in MTRL, rather than chance fluctuations or architecture-specific quirks. The credit is at the generalization layer: the conclusion's claim that sparsification reduces plasticity-loss indicators is undergirded by a robustness check that typical single-architecture or single-benchmark studies lack.

nodes.title: Multi-architecture, multi-benchmark consistency of plasticity indicator patterns

nodes.content: All three plasticity indicators are defined with explicit mathematical formulae: dormant neuron percentage uses normalized activation s_i^l = E|h_i^l| / (1/H^l Σ E|h_k^l|) with threshold τ (dormant if s_i^l ≤ τ); effective rank uses singular value proportion srank_δ(Φ) = min_k {Σ_{i=1}^k σ_i / Σ_{i=1}^d σ_i ≥ 1-δ}; Fisher trace is Tr(F) = E_{s,a∼π}[||∇_θ log π(a|s)||²₂]. These definitions are consistent with prior literature (Sokar et al., 2023 for dormant neurons; Klein et al., 2024 for effective rank; Falzari & Sabatelli, 2025 for Fisher trace).

metadata.credit: By grounding the plasticity indicators in established definitions from the recent plasticity loss literature, the paper preempts the failure mode where ad-hoc or underspecified metrics would be uninterpretable or non-reproducible. The definitions enable other researchers to replicate the measurements exactly, and the consistency with prior work allows readers to relate the reported indicator values to known patterns (e.g., dormant neuron thresholds, effective rank tolerance). This provides credit at the measurement layer: the conclusion that sparsification affects these indicators rests on metrics that are standard in the field, not proprietary or ambiguous.

refs.text: Sokar et al. 2023; Klein et al. 2024; Falzari & Sabatelli 2025

nodes.title: Precise mathematical definitions for plasticity indicators

nodes.content: All aggregated performance results across MiniGrid benchmarks (Table 1 and learning curves in Appendix F) report normalized interquantile mean (IQM) with 95% confidence intervals computed via stratified bootstrap using the rliable library (Agarwal et al., 2021). This replaces scalar means with a distribution-robust location estimator and quantifies uncertainty through non-parametric resampling across 30 independent seeds.

metadata.credit: This guards against the common failure mode in RL evaluation where mean returns are reported without error bars, making it impossible to assess whether visible differences are credible. The use of stratified bootstrap CIs with IQM provides a principled approach recommended by the RL statistical best practices literature. It underwrites the conclusion that sparse agents outperform dense baselines by supplying a quantitative measure of uncertainty: whenever the CIs do not overlap (e.g., MT5 MTPPO: dense 0.61-0.71 vs GMP 0.75-0.86), the difference is statistically discernible; when they overlap, the paper's claims are appropriately hedged. The credit is at the uncertainty quantification layer, making the performance comparisons more interpretable and trustworthy than a simple table of mean returns.

nodes.title: Use of IQM with stratified bootstrap confidence intervals for all performance comparisons

nodes.content: The paper evaluates GMP and SET on three architecturally distinct MTRL models (MTPPO: shared backbone with task-specific heads; MoE: mixture of experts; MOORE: mixture of orthogonal experts) using the same hyperparameters (learning rate, network size, optimizer, sparsity level 95%) and the same three benchmarks, enabling direct attribution of differential outcomes (e.g., SET reducing performance in MOORE but not in MTPPO/MoE) to architectural design rather than confounding by training setup.

metadata.credit: This controlled comparison preempts the failure mode where an observed architecture-sparsification interaction could be explained by different hyperparameter choices across architectures (e.g., MOORE using a higher learning rate that makes pruning unstable). By holding non-architectural factors constant, the paper isolates the architecture as the modulator of sparsification benefit. This underwrites the conclusion that sparsification benefits are architecture-dependent at the qualitative direction layer: the evidence does not just show that MOORE performs differently; it shows that under identical conditions, the effect of sparsification on performance flips sign (from positive to neutral/slightly negative for SET). The scope of credit is bounded to the compared architectures but provides a strong case for architecture-dependence.

nodes.title: Systematic evaluation of three architectures with identical hyperparameters reveals interaction with sparsification

nodes.content: In the MetaWorld MT10 continuous-control experiment, the paper compares three conditions: dense MTMH-SAC, GMP applied to both actor and critic (global pruning), and GMP applied only to the actor (selective actor pruning). All other training aspects (replay buffer, learning rate, architecture size, total timesteps, evaluation protocol) are kept identical across conditions. This design isolates the contribution of actor pruning from the confound of global sparsification (which also prunes the critic, potentially harming value estimation as noted by McLean et al. 2025).

metadata.credit: The three-condition design guards against the failure mode where an observed improvement from sparsification could be attributed to any form of pruning rather than to selective actor pruning. By showing that global pruning (actor+critic) yields only a 75% success rate compared to actor-only pruning at 81% (with non-overlapping CIs), the paper demonstrates that the benefit is not merely from pruning per se but from the selective sparing of critic capacity. This provides causal-evidential credit at the mechanism/attribution layer: the conclusion that selective actor pruning is beneficial is supported by a contrast that rules out the alternative explanation that any form of sparsification would work. The controlled comparison is a strength that goes beyond simply reporting correlations.

nodes.title: Controlled three-condition experiment isolating the effect of actor pruning from global pruning

nodes.content: On MTPPO with MT5, the paper reports not only final IQM (Figure 6 and accompanying text) but also learning curves for all four plasticity indicators (Fisher trace, effective rank, actor dormant %, critic dormant %) for GMP, GMP+WD, GMP+PCGrad, and PCGrad alone (Figure 7). This allows both performance and mechanistic comparison under the same seeds and training conditions.

metadata.credit: The dual reporting of performance and plasticity indicators preempts the failure mode where a combination method might match GMP's performance but via different plasticity mechanisms (e.g., PCGrad might improve performance without changing plasticity indicators, suggesting a different route). By showing that PCGrad alone improves performance over dense but does not alter plasticity indicators, and that GMP+PCGrad barely changes plasticity indicators relative to GMP alone, the paper provides evidence that GMP's plasticity effects dominate in the combined setting. This underwrites the conclusion that no additive benefit exists by demonstrating that the combination does not improve either performance or plasticity indicators beyond GMP alone. The credit is at the measurement complexity layer: the paper does not just compare final scores but checks whether the combination changes the underlying dynamics.

nodes.title: Comprehensive plasticity and performance comparison across GMP, GMP+WD, GMP+PCGrad, and PCGrad alone

nodes.content: The qualitative pattern of GMP producing a transient Fisher trace increase followed by a decline to low values, while SET maintains low stable Fisher trace values throughout training, is observed not just on MTPPO on MT5 but also on MoE and MOORE architectures and across MT3, MT5, and MT7 benchmarks (Figures 16-21 in Appendix G), providing replication across six architecture-benchmark combinations for both GMP and SET.

metadata.credit: This replication across architectures and benchmarks guards against the failure mode where the claimed distinct dynamics could be artifacts of a specific architecture or environment (e.g., MTPPO's shared backbone causing Fisher trace peaks that do not appear in MoE). By showing that the peak-and-decline for GMP and stable-low for SET appear in all three architectures and three benchmarks, the paper strengthens the case that these are genuine dynamical properties of the sparsification methods themselves rather than interactions with specific network designs. The credit is at the generalization layer: the conclusion that the dynamics are distinct and robust is better supported than if it were observed only in a single configuration.

nodes.title: Cross-architecture replication of GMP peak-and-decline and SET stable-low Fisher trace patterns

nodes.content: On MT5 (and replicated on MT3 and MT7 in Appendix G), the paper shows simultaneously that LayerNorm reduces actor and critic dormant neuron percentages to near-zero (lower than any sparse method or dense baseline) but collapses the effective rank of the shared feature extractor to values near 1 (Figure 5). This trade-off is demonstrated across all three architectures (MTPPO, MoE, MOORE), and the poor final IQM values (Table 1: IQM 0.28-0.60 vs best 0.76-0.87) are consistently observed.

metadata.credit: This guard against the failure mode where a simple reduction in dormant neurons is taken as evidence of improved plasticity regardless of representational quality. By measuring both dormancy and effective rank simultaneously, the paper reveals that normalization can suppress dormancy at the cost of collapsing representational diversity—a trade-off that would be missed by monitoring only one indicator. The replication across three architectures and three benchmarks provides evidence that this is not a specific implementation fluke. The credit is at the qualitative direction layer: the conclusion that LayerNorm's apparent dormancy benefits are outweighed by rank collapse is directly and consistently supported by the joint measurement.

nodes.title: Direct empirical demonstration of the trade-off between dormancy reduction and rank collapse under LayerNorm

steps.reasoning:
Define Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP) as the pruning schedule that progressively increases network sparsity during training by masking (setting to zero) connections with the smallest absolute magnitudes at regular pruning intervals; the sparsity level at training timestep $t$ is
$$
\rho_{t}=
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } t<t_{\text{start}}, \\
\rho_{F}\left[1-\left(1-\frac{t-t_{\text{start}}}{t_{\text{end}}-t_{\text{start}}}\right)^{3}\right] & \text{if } t_{\text{start}} \le t \le t_{\text{end}}, \\
\rho_{F} & \text{if } t>t_{\text{end}}.
\end{cases}
$$
Here $\rho_F$ denotes the final target sparsity, and $t_{\text{start}}, t_{\text{end}}$ are the pruning window bounds; this implementation follows the cited GMP schedule. 
Zhu & Gupta (2017)
